text: {"answer": "Nuclear power appears to be a useful tool for cutting carbon emissions, though its cost-effectiveness and construction risks are contested. Supporting evidence says nuclear plants emit no greenhouse gases during operation and have life-cycle emissions similar to wind and about a third of solar per unit of electricity [8ef6c9360938#3]. The IAEA links higher nuclear output, alongside renewables and coal-to-gas switching, to a levelling of global CO2 emissions [7e88e103d8fb#0]. A 16-country study found that cutting CO2 by 1% required a 2.907% increase in nuclear generation versus 4.902% for renewables, concluding nuclear is more cost-efficient even counting accident risks [0819b42abe08#0][946b45d61e84#2]. The contradicting side is substantial: the same cost study is a single dataset, and a Swedish model found little cost benefit from reinvesting in nuclear once existing plants retire [6b0ccdbcf9aa#1]. Nuclear construction often overruns costs, with an average overrun of 102.5% reported [06384d0fb532#2], and critics cite health, accident and waste risks [4e9b20313655#3]. Overall, nuclear is a strong low-carbon option, but its economic case depends on cost and delivery.", "confidence": 62, "one_line": "Nuclear is low-carbon and possibly cost-efficient for CO2 cuts, but construction overruns and cost disputes temper the case."}
